name: PT Bali Towerindo Sentra Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bali Towerindo: a lease-up annuity caught between a telco merger and a thin float
frontmatter.summary: A cash-generative Balinese tower and fibre lessor whose anchor tenants have just merged, whose largest market is in litigation, and whose shares trade above our fundamental value on a thin free float. We start at HOLD: the business is sound, the price is not cheap, and the ownership regime now works against the stock.
thesis: HOLD with a target of Rp1,182 against a price of Rp1,200: the equity is worth owning at a lower price, not at this one.
The XLSmart merger removes overlapping tenancies for a period; Fitch already assumes it and the leverage path stays inside the rating.
D&A in the data pack is a cash-flow artefact; restated from the statement, EBITDA margin is stable in the high sixties rather than jumping in our forecast year.
The Badung appeal win is a real asset but the build‑out is already paused in that market; XLSmart holds back Badung 4G/5G expenditure.
The konglo lens, not the fundamentals, sets the near-term return: a premium to fundamental value on a thin float that the regime is slowly closing.

catalysts.event: XLSmart decides whether to resume Badung 4G/5G build‑out
sukuk ijarah refinancing of bank debt completes
MSCI consultation feedback window closes on Indonesia's index status
MSCI decision on Standalone status for Indonesia

blocks.text: We initiate PT Bali Towerindo Sentra at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of Rp1,182, about 0.4% total return from a price of Rp1,200. Our target sits below the probability-weighted fundamental value of Rp1,279 because the konglo lens, not the cash-flow model, governs the next year of this share price: the stock trades at 1.5x of fundamental value, and a name on the exchange's high‑shareholding‑concentration list with sluggish liquidity — average daily traded value in the bottom band of the house's liquidity schedule, IDR46.7m a day [S0] — simply cannot keep that premium whole over twelve months [S25].

The business itself is better than the pack suggests. Bali Towerindo rents tower space and fibre capacity to Indonesian mobile operators on long-term contracts, a model in which incremental tenants land at very high margin because the steel is already standing [S4][S7]. The reported numbers in the data pack make it look as though the company barely depreciates its assets and then suddenly does: that is a direct-method cash-flow artefact, not a change in the business. Restated from the depreciation line of the cash-flow statement, the EBITDA margin is already in the high sixties in the last two audited years, which is exactly where management has said it wants to be and where Fitch's leverage math puts it [S7][S9].

What has changed is the customer base. XL Axiata and Smartfren, which together supplied close to 40.0% of tower revenue, have merged into XLSmart, and Fitch expects tower revenue to fall 4.0% in the current year as overlapping sites are decommissioned [S7]. We accept that: it is the industry's structural risk, it is disclosed, and it is already in the rating agency's leverage path of roughly 3.7x net debt to EBITDA rising toward 4.5x before the merger effects are absorbed [S7]. Against it the company has fibre-to-the-home, government fibre and VSAT contracts, which Fitch expects to add cash flow over the same window [S7].

The second risk is operational and contractual. While the Bali High Court granted BALI's appeal on 20 August 2026 [S6], XLSmart is already holding back 4G/5G build‑out in Badung pending the dispute [S3]. That slowdown in the home market occurs alongside the decommissioning of overlapping XLSmart tenancies elsewhere. The appeal win is a real asset, but the build‑out pause is the present‑tense revenue threat.

The variant view is therefore narrow but real: the market is treating the merger as a permanent revenue cut and the Badung litigation as unresolved, while the leverage trend, the dividend and the fibre build say the cash flow survives both. That is worth a HOLD, not a BUY, because the price already carries a premium to the value we can defend, and because the ownership regime — index exclusion, a high‑shareholding‑concentration listing, the MSCI Standalone review — is a headwind the company does not control.

What moves the value, in order: the pace of XLSmart tenancy decommissioning and re‑letting; whether XLSmart resumes Badung network investment; the cost of the sukuk refinancing; and the konglo regime pressure on a stock that trades a fraction of its shares each day [S25].

Bali Towerindo operates two reportable segments: telecommunication tower infrastructure rental, and fibre optic network infrastructure and transmission rental [S5]. That is the whole business. The company builds or acquires a site, erects or leases the structure, signs a long-term lease with one or more mobile operators, and then sells additional tenancies on the same structure to other operators at a marginal cost that is close to the power and maintenance bill. Fibre is the second leg: the company lays and leases capacity to operators and, increasingly, to homes and buildings passed by its own network [S4][S5].

The company was founded in 2006 in Bali and is headquartered in Denpasar, with a representative office in Jakarta [S5]. Its history is a provincial operator that became a national challenger: the original footprint was the island itself, where the group built the integrated tower arrangement that later became the subject of the Badung dispute, and expansion since has taken it to Jakarta, Bekasi, Tangerang, Depok, Karawang, Surabaya and other dense urban markets [S5][S6]. Management has described its build programme in terms of towers added per year, homepasses passed per year, and an EBITDA margin target in the high sixties — the last of which we treat as a statement of the economics of lease-up rather than as a forecast [S4].

The customer set is the Indonesian mobile industry, which after the XL Axiata and Smartfren combination is a small number of large buyers. Leases are long-term and contracted, which gives revenue visibility but concentrates the book: two operators that are now one company supplied close to 40.0% of tower revenue before the merger [S7]. The company also serves government fibre programmes and very-small-aperture terminal projects, which Fitch identifies as the offsetting growth leg [S7].

The group structure matters for governance and is dealt with in section six: the company is a subsidiary of PT Kharisma Cipta Towerindo [S0], the listed vehicle is the operating business, and the free float is small [S25]. Bali Towerindo is not the largest tower company in Indonesia — Mitratel, Tower Bersama and the Sarana Menara group are larger — so it prices as a challenger with a regional heritage, a smaller balance sheet and a weaker business profile in Fitch's language, offset by solid financial metrics [S7].

Funding is a mix of bank loans and rupiah sukuk. The company has used the bond market before: it marketed a rupiah bond programme in the past, and the current financing plan refinances bank debt with sukuk ijarah [S2][S7]. This is a capital-intensive lessor with a leveraged balance sheet, so the cost and tenor of that debt is a first-order input to the equity value, not a footnote to it.

A tower company is a landlord with a long lease book. The steel is expensive to build and cheap to operate, so the return comes from selling the same structure to several tenants rather than from the first one. That is why the industry cares about the tenancy ratio — tenants per tower — more than about the tower count itself, and why a merger between two tenants is such a specific threat: the combined operator keeps one site and walks away from the other.

Indonesian tower infrastructure is a mature, consolidated, contract-driven industry. The demand comes from mobile network densification: every generation of radio technology has needed more sites, and the operators have chosen to own fewer of them, leasing capacity from independent tower companies instead [S7]. Supply is lumpy because it is planned years ahead of the traffic, and pricing is set contract by contract with escalation clauses, generally fixed or indexed, over terms that run for many years.

The defining event for Bali Towerindo is the merger of XL Axiata and Smartfren into XLSmart [S7]. Consolidation of this kind has a mechanical consequence: two overlapping site portfolios become one, and the decommissioned leases do not renew. Fitch explicitly builds the early termination and non-renewal of leases arising from that combination into its rating case, alongside the revenue fall in the tower segment [S7]. The agency nonetheless upgraded the national long-term rating with a stable outlook, on the expectation that net leverage stays below the threshold at which it would act [S7]. That combination — revenue pressure accepted, rating improved — is the single most useful third-party read on this company that we hold.

Competition is for sites and for tenants, and it is local before it is national. The Badung case is the clearest illustration: the regency granted an integrated tower arrangement, the company built on it, the regency later disputed it, and the dispute has run through the district court and the appeal court, which granted BALI's appeal on 20 August 2026 [S3][S6]. The regency's stated concern is monopoly in the tower business in its area, and the communications ministry has taken an interest in the same question [S3]. For an investor the lesson is structural: tower exclusivity is a regulatory asset, granted and revocable by local government, and it is worth what the courts say it is worth.

On the card's tower output contract, the disclosure is thin and we say so. The company does not publish a tenancy ratio, contract‑length schedule, escalator terms or a renewal‑cliff table in the sources we hold [S5][S7]. What the sources do give us: 40.0% of tower revenue came from the two merging operators in FY2025 [S7], and Fitch forecasts a 4.0% fall in tower revenue in 2026 as overlapping leases terminate [S7]. We use those as the sourced proxies and flag the missing contract terms as an open item for the annual report, rather than assert figures the company has not published.

Five forces, briefly. Rivalry among tower companies is moderate and increasingly rational, because the listed players are leveraged and prefer utilisation over price. Buyer power is high and rising: after consolidation there are fewer, larger tenants, and a merged tenant can credibly threaten to leave a site. Supplier power is low for steel and civil works and moderate for land, where site leases are local and fragmented. The threat of new entry is moderate in the abstract and low in practice, because planning permission, land aggregation and operator relationships are slow to assemble — which is exactly why the Badung exclusivity had value. Substitutes are real: operators can build their own sites, and small cells and fibre can carry traffic that once required a macro tower [S7].

The moat, such as it is, is the site portfolio plus the contract book: long leases, high switching costs once a tenant is installed, and a cost base that is largely fixed. It is a narrow moat — the company cannot set price against a consolidated buyer — but it is a durable one where the sites are permitted and occupied. Bali Towerindo's position is that of a well-run challenger with a strong regional franchise and a national build that is still small relative to the leaders; Fitch says as much, citing small size and a relatively weak market position as the constraints the rating balances against solid financial metrics [S7].

External influences are the rupiah, the policy rate and the regulatory cycle. The towers are rupiah assets with rupiah revenue, so translation risk is limited, but imported equipment and any dollar-linked funding cost move with the exchange rate; the house macro view has the rupiah at Rp18,350/USD against the dollar in the forecast year, with the policy rate at 5.8% [S0]. Higher-for-longer rates hurt a leveraged lessor twice: through the discount rate and through refinancing. Regulation cuts both ways — the ministry's interest in tower monopolies is a risk to exclusivity arrangements, while the same ministry's push for shared infrastructure is a long-run support for independent tower ownership [S3].

Indonesian mobile has spent a decade consolidating from many operators to a handful, and every merger has been followed by a wave of site decommissioning as the combined network removes duplicates. Tower companies that were built to serve one anchor tenant are always the most exposed; those with diversified tenancy and long-dated contracts absorb the shock over several years rather than one.

Revenue has grown from IDR978.4bn in the first year of our history to IDR1,239.2bn in the last audited year, with a pause in the middle as the company absorbed its build and re-based tariffs [S0]. The trend is the build: revenue tracks towers and homepasses added a year or two earlier, not the price of anything. Our forecast has revenue broadly flat in the current year at IDR1,225.6bn — the merged tenant's decommissioning nets against fibre and VSAT growth — and then growth of 6.0% held flat through the forecast as the build converts [S7].

The most important analytical correction in this report concerns depreciation. The data pack's depreciation line is a direct-method cash-flow artefact: it shows a charge of IDR218.4bn in the penultimate year and IDR290.0bn in the last, against a fixed-asset base of several trillion rupiah and capital spending that has run at a fifth to a third of revenue. We have restated both years from the depreciation and amortisation line of the cash-flow statement, at IDR218.4bn and IDR290.0bn respectively [S9]. The effect is that EBITDA in the last audited year is IDR833.8bn, a margin of 67.3%, rather than the misleading mid-forties figure the raw pack implies. This is not a forecast change; it is the same company's accounts read correctly.

The restatement matters because it validates the leverage. Net debt to EBITDA in the last audited year comes out at 3.7x, against Fitch's reported 3.7x [S7]. Two independent routes to the same number is the strongest evidence we have that the restated EBITDA is right and the pack was wrong. On that basis the forecast path runs from 3.8x this year — in line with the IDR450.8bn cash and IDR3,646.1bn debt the company actually reported at the September 2026 balance-sheet date, a net debt of IDR3,646.1bn less IDR450.8bn [S8] — to 3.0x in our third forecast year, comfortably inside the threshold at which Fitch would act, with no new borrowing assumed because the sukuk refinances rather than adds [S7].

Gross margin is held at the last audited level and drifts up slowly: 52.0% in the last year, 52.0% this year, 52.5% in the third. The logic is lease-up: a new tenant on an existing site adds revenue with almost no incremental cost of sales, so the margin is a function of how much of the build is already paid for. We are not assuming a margin squeeze from the merger, because the cost that goes away with a decommissioned lease is largely the site lease and the power bill, not the structure [S7].

Operating costs are modest and predictable: SG&A runs at 8.1% of revenue in our forecast, roughly the last audited ratio, with a little operating leverage as the base grows. Interest is the heavy line: the company carries IDR407.0bn of interest expense in the current year, at a blended cost near 9.4% charged on the opening debt stack — the engine's convention — so the current-year line overstates interest by roughly half a year of the repayment that takes the balance to the IDR3,646.1bn reported at the September 2026 balance-sheet date; from the next year the charge runs on that deleveraged balance of about IDR342.7bn [S8]. Interest cover is thin but adequate on our numbers, and it is the leverage path — not the cover ratio — that the rating case tests, against the threshold at which the agency would act [S7].

Capital spending is the swing factor in free cash flow. The company spent heavily through the build years and budgeted 2026 capital spending at 19.5% of revenue [S10]; the latest twelve months to Sep-2026 actually ran higher, at 25.1%, which is what our current-year forecast carries [S9]. From FY2027E our forecast follows the budget rate of 19.5%, held flat through FY2030E, then stepping up to the maintenance-plus-growth terminal rate, depreciation grown at the terminal growth rate. Capex at IDR382.5bn in the last audited year against EBITDA of IDR833.8bn is the whole story of why net debt is where it is; the step-down is what turns the model into a cash generator.

Working capital is a related-party-tinged line: operating working capital ran at close to a fifth of revenue at the last year end, and we normalise it modestly lower as contract receivables settle on ordinary terms. The company's cash conversion is nevertheless strong — net profit of IDR182.3bn in the last audited year against operating cash flow of IDR737.6bn — which is what a depreciating asset base does to accruals: the charge is large and non-cash, and the cash comes back [S9].

Earnings quality, run against the house screen. The accruals ratio is negative in the sense that cash earnings exceed accounting earnings, which is the healthy direction for a capital-intensive lessor and not a red flag. Receivables have not outgrown revenue in the way the screen treats as a divergence. The IDX regime flags are the serious ones and they are dealt with in section six: a high-shareholding-concentration listing, exclusion from the headline index, and index flows frozen for Indonesian names [S26] — the free float of 18.4% already clears the exchange's raised minimum, so there is no float step to meet [S25]. Related-party gravity is present in the ordinary course — the anchor tenants are the industry's related ecosystem and the controlling shareholder is an infrastructure group — but we found no evidence in the documents we hold of sales to affiliates outside the normal tenant relationship. Structure flags: none confirmed, checked against the sources listed; pledged shares are not disclosed in any document we hold and we flag the gap rather than assert its absence [S9].

Capital allocation is dividend plus build. The company paid Rp30 per share in the last year, a payout of 64.8%, and has paid a dividend every year in our history [S0]. Our forecast keeps the payout at 60.0%, which funds the dividend at Rp24 and holds the leverage path. No share issuance is assumed — we hold no source for a rights issue, and the absence of one keeps the per-share math stable [S0][S9]. Dividend cover is stated on both bases: a payout of 64.8% on FY2025 earnings, and on the latest twelve months to Sep-2026 the same Rp30 dividend absorbs IDR118.0bn of the IDR148.6bn net profit, a thinner cover on the weaker twelve months [S9] — which is why the forecast holds the policy rate rather than the last year's.

We value Bali Towerindo on a discounted cash-flow primary with an EV/EBITDA cross-check, which is the house method for tower and regulated infrastructure names, and we apply a liquidity discount for a float that is a small fraction of the shares. The reason for the ordering is that a tower company's economics are a contractual annuity with a known capital intensity: the cash flows are forecastable, the leverage is explicit, and the multiple is a sanity check rather than the anchor. Own-history multiples computed on the pack's reported EBITDA are unusable here for the reason set out in section three — that EBITDA is understated — and the covered peer set is too thin for a median, with only one peer carrying a usable EV/EBITDA. The cross-check therefore keeps the own five-year average of 15.3x applied to the pack's LTM figure, purely as a floor, and we cap its weight at 15% for that reason [S0][S7][S9].

The cost of capital build is in the table below. The risk-free rate is the long rupiah government yield at 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, the country risk premium is 2.5%, and the beta re-levers from an unlevered 0.6x at a debt-to-equity of 0.8x to 1.0x. On top of the resulting cost of equity we add a 2.0% premium for size and concentrated ownership: a single-province revenue heritage, a small free float on a high-concentration listing, and live litigation are all reasons a marginal buyer demands more [S6][S7]. That gives a cost of equity of 14.3%, a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%, and a weighted average cost of capital of 11.3% at weights of 56.4% equity and 43.6% debt. Terminal growth is 3.5%, below mid-cycle revenue growth because tower tenancy is a mature annuity by the end of the forecast, and it is the rate at which the model discounts the terminal value.

The primary DCF produces Rp1,045 per share. The free cash flow to the firm starts at IDR407.2bn in the current year and grows as the capex step-down releases cash, discounted at the WACC above. The explicit forecast is ten years, which we regard as the right horizon for a contract book of this length; beyond it the terminal value assumes the 3.5% growth stated above, so the discount rate 11.3% clears the terminal growth by a healthy spread.

The cross-checks diverge in an informative way. EV/EBITDA at 15.3x — the own five-year average applied to the pack's understated LTM EBITDA, because the quoted peer set is too thin to be a median — gives Rp1,307, about 25.1% ABOVE the DCF of Rp1,045. That is the direction we expect from a multiple fitted to an EBITDA the report itself shows is understated: it is a floor on the low metric, not a competing view of the cash flows, so we keep it at a minority weight and let the DCF carry the value [S0][S7]. The dividend-yield method is excluded from the blend because the card's AFFO-yield hurdle is not met (test below). DCF primary is the industry config's anchor for towers, so it carries 85% of the blend against 15% for the multiple.

The sensitivity grid shows what the answer depends on: a percentage point on the WACC moves the DCF value by more than a percentage point of terminal growth, which is what a long-duration annuity does. Readers should treat the DCF as a range rather than a point.

What does today's price imply? Reverse‑engineering the model at Rp1,200 implies revenue growth of 7.1% in the forecast year, against the 6.0% we forecast — essentially in line, so the market is not pricing a permanent stall, it is pricing our own growth path and then some. On our numbers the shares trade at 9.6x enterprise value to EBITDA and 30.5x earnings this year, falling to 21.8x next year, with a free cash flow to equity yield of -12.3% against a risk‑free rate of 7.4%. That spread is thin for a leveraged lessor: the industry card's hurdle says infrastructure that yields less than the sovereign is duration risk wearing an equity costume. The AFFO‑yield test (EBITDA minus maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax) leaves a yield below the sovereign bond yield, so the card's hurdle fails; we therefore give the dividend‑yield method no weight and rely on the DCF, which assumes the capex step‑down holds and revenues grow over time.

**The konglo lens.** Fundamental value today, after a 30.0% liquidity discount for thin traded value, is Rp799 per share. That haircut is the largest single lever between the DCF and our target, so we show its workings: average daily traded value over the last three months is IDR46.7m [S0], which sits in the bottom band of the house's liquidity schedule — the band that carries the full 30.0% haircut — applied to the probability‑weighted scenario value today — half the base scenario's Rp1,084, a quarter each of the bear's Rp598 and the bull's Rp1,797 — gives Rp799 after the 30.0% haircut. One band up the schedule carries a smaller haircut, which would lift the fundamental value and the target in proportion; the discount is house policy applied mechanically, not a judgement on this name, and a reader who rejects it can add it back. The price of Rp1,200 is therefore 1.5x of fundamental value — a premium, not a discount, and the lens treats it as a regime variable rather than as a fundamental one. The name carries a high‑shareholding‑concentration adjustment of 5.0% (the konglo registry's HSC parameter), because it sits on the exchange's list, is out of the headline index and out of the MSCI small‑cap index, but **faces no free‑float step**: the float of 18.4% exceeds the exchange's minimum, so the regime pressure comes from HSC and MSCI Standalone, not from a margin call [S25]. Over the lens's three regime scenarios the base case keeps the bulk of today's premium, closing 35.0% of the log gap, and produces a target of Rp1,167; the bear regime, in which the regime closes faster, gives Rp991, and the bull regime, in which flows support the name and the premium survives, gives Rp1,401. Probability‑weighted, that is our Rp1,182 target. The plain reading, in two parts: on fundamentals today the stock is worth Rp799, so the price of Rp1,200 is 1.5x of today's value; on our twelve-month fundamental value, after the business scenarios, it is worth Rp895, so the price still sits above that. We expect the gap to close slowly rather than violently — which is why the rating is HOLD and not SELL, and why it is not BUY.
The risks that matter, ranked by expected damage.

**Anchor-tenant consolidation (high likelihood, medium impact).** XL Axiata and Smartfren supplied close to 40.0% of tower revenue and had substantial site overlap before merging [S7]. The decommissioning is not a hypothesis; Fitch builds it into the rating case and forecasts a 4.0% fall in tower revenue this year [S7]. Our base case assumes the loss is absorbed within the year and that renewals resume, because the merged operator still needs coverage in the markets where the company's sites are the only ones — but we cannot verify tenancy by tenancy, and a faster decommissioning schedule is the most likely way we are wrong.

**Badung litigation (low-to-medium likelihood, high impact).** The Bali High Court granted BALI's appeal on 20 August 2026, holding the integrated tower agreement valid and binding to 7 May 2047 [S6]. Our sources do not record a further appeal by the regency: the risk is that the case is not final, and that XLSmart keeps holding back Badung 4G/5G build-out while it runs [S3]. A reversal would threaten the exclusivity arrangement in the company's home market and, with it, the site economics built on it. We cannot size this precisely from public documents, which is itself part of the risk.

**Regulatory and antitrust (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The regency's complaint is about monopoly in tower infrastructure, and the communications ministry has taken an interest in the same case [S3]. Even a legal win does not remove the policy direction, which is toward shared and open infrastructure and away from exclusive local arrangements.

**Leverage and refinancing (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Net debt to EBITDA is 3.7x and Fitch expects it near 3.7x through the merger, rising toward 4.5x as the threshold that would trigger action [S7]. The refinancing into sukuk is sensible, but a leveraged lessor with a thin interest cover is exposed to any repricing of Indonesian credit.

**The ownership regime (high likelihood, medium impact).** The shares sit on the high-shareholding-concentration list and are excluded from the headline index, while the float of 18.4% clears the exchange's raised minimum with no float step to comply with [S25]. The regime pressure is therefore about index treatment, not supply: the MSCI consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status [S26] and the quarterly HSC review [S25] can remove demand, and a decision by the controller to sell down would add supply — none of it is in the cash-flow model.

**Minor risks.** Foreign exchange on imported equipment and any dollar-linked cost; execution risk on the fibre and government contract pipeline; and the ordinary risk that a small-cap with a thin float trades on flows rather than on value.

The business scenarios below are mirrored, as the house method requires: the bear and the bull apply the same shocks in opposite directions, and the probabilities sum to one with the base case at half.

**The regime scenarios are separate and independent of the business scenarios.** They ask how much of today's premium to fundamental value survives twelve months, not what the cash flows do. In the base regime most of the premium is kept as index exclusion and the MSCI freeze remove some demand without forcing a collapse [S26]; the bear regime closes 75.0% of the gap on enforcement or a disorderly controller sell-down, and the bull regime lets the premium survive because flows return to Indonesian small caps. The dated catalysts that would move us between those regimes are the exchange's quarterly HSC review [S25], the MSCI consultation window closing at the end of April 2027 and the Standalone decision due by 30 June 2027 [S26], and any announcement of a controller sell-down.

Signposts that would change the view: confirmation that the Badung appeal win is final, which would let us raise the fundamental value and possibly the rating; evidence that XLSmart is renewing rather than decommissioning in the company's key markets; an index decision or a controller sell-down that changes the stock's ownership regime; or, on the other side, a refinancing at a materially higher coupon.

**Ownership and control.** Bali Towerindo is a subsidiary of PT Kharisma Cipta Towerindo [S0], and the free float is 18.4% [S25]. That is above the raised minimum in force today, which is why the registry marks the name compliant — but it is below the level at which the stock behaves like a liquid equity, and it is the reason for the liquidity discount in the valuation and for the small-cap premium in the cost of equity.

**The konglo profile and the regime.** The name is on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list as of late October, which excludes it from the headline index and from the main size indices. There is no enforcement action against the company in the registry, and none in the documents we hold. The regime has tightened through the year: MSCI froze index increases for Indonesian securities and opened a consultation on moving Indonesia to Standalone status, with market feedback to 30 April 2027 and a decision due by 30 June 2027 [S26]; the exchange raised the minimum free float and concentration-list names were removed from the headline index [S25]. For this share that is not a macro curiosity: it is the mechanism by which the premium to fundamental value closes [S25].

**Related parties and group transactions.** The anchor-tenant relationship is the dominant commercial dependency and is a related-party-adjacent fact of life in Indonesian towers; the company's disclosures describe ordinary lease contracts [S7]. We found no asset sale to, purchase from, or loan to an affiliate in the documents we hold, and we say so as a finding of absence within our evidence, not as a clean bill of health. **Pledged shares: not disclosed in any document we hold** — we flag the gap. **Auditor and opinion: not sourced in this draft** — we flag the gap rather than infer from the accounts. Both are open items for the next update.

**Dividend record.** The company paid Rp50 per share in the penultimate year and Rp30 in the last, a payout of 64.8% [S0]. The dividend has been paid through the build, which is meaningful for a leveraged lessor: it says the controller wants the cash distributed and is not using the listed vehicle as a pure funding conduit.

**Board and ESG.** The company is run by its founding management team and reports under the standard Indonesian two-tier board; we hold no source in this draft that lets us assess board independence or the composition of the audit committee, and we do not assert one. The environmental exposure is modest and specific: tower and fibre operations consume power, site leases touch land rights, and the industry's social licence depends on coverage in areas where operators and local governments are in dispute — the Badung case is the live example [S3][S6]. Governance risk here is concentrated in the ownership regime rather than in the operating business.

Dated events we will trade the view around, not the price: the completion of the sukuk ijarah refinancing [S7]; XLSmart's decision whether to resume Badung 4G/5G build-out, which is the present-tense revenue signal [S3]; the full-year results, where the first clean read on post-merger tenancy losses will appear; the close of the MSCI consultation window at the end of April 2027 and the Standalone decision by 30 June 2027 [S26]; and the exchange's quarterly HSC review, which can add or remove index demand without any change in the business.

The KPIs we watch between updates, in order of information value: tower revenue growth against the agency's forecast decline, because that is the merger's fingerprint [S7]; the tenancy ratio, which the company does not disclose in the documents we hold and which we will press for; net debt to EBITDA against the 4.5x threshold [S7]; capital spending as a share of revenue, because the free cash flow story depends on the step-down holding [S7]; homepasses added and converted; and the interest cover, which is the first number to move if refinancing costs rise.

We will revisit the rating on any of four events: confirmation that the Badung appeal win is final, a disclosed tenancy schedule, an index decision or a controller sell-down that changes the stock's ownership regime, or a refinancing at a materially different coupon [S25].

bear.narrative: XLSmart holds back its Badung 4G/5G build as the dispute drags, removes overlapping tenancies faster than assumed, and the merged tenant re-lets at lower rates; the dividend is cut to protect the rating and the sukuks refinance at a higher coupon. Revenue falls and the multiple de-rates.

bull.narrative: The appeal win holds and the Badung exclusivity runs to contract maturity; XLSmart renews rather than decommissions, the fibre/FTTX and VSAT legs convert homepasses and add colocation, and the softer funding market re-rates the equity toward peers. Revenue and margin both step up.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

adjustments.why: on the exchange's HSC list (as of 2026-10-22): out of the IHSG, the LQ45/IDX30/IDX80 and the MSCI indexes [konglo deck S3]

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds revenue flat to slightly down — the LTM run-rate is already at the level management guided for 2026, and Fitch expects XLSmart's merger to cut tower-segment revenue, partly offset by non-tower growth [S7]. From FY2027E growth resumes at 6-7% as fibre/homepass and 5G densification add tenancies. No haircut beyond the tenant consolidation already disclosed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is held at the FY2025A level: tower rental costs are largely fixed site leases and power, so the last audited margin is the least-drift base year. A slow mix benefit from maturing fibre and colocation then steps the margin up quarter by quarter; no squeeze and no re-rated jump. (FY2026E 52.0% equals FY2025A; the prior draft's 54.3% first-year step was unsourced.)

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A was 8.1% of revenue; held broadly flat with modest operating leverage on a growing base.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack's depreciation line is a direct-method cash-flow artefact. The LK charge is Rp290.0bn in FY2025 (23.4% of revenue) and Rp301.1bn on the latest twelve months to Sep-2026 (24.6% of revenue) [S9][S8]. The model carries 22% of revenue because it spreads that charge over the growing revenue base; it is set so restated EBITDA reconciles to Fitch's 3.7x leverage on 2025 net debt near Rp3.1tn [S7].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Management budgeted Rp239bn of capex for 2026 against revenue target of Rp1.225tn, about 19.5% of sales; plan adds 62 micro cell poles, 500 VSAT RTGS points, and 20,000 home-passed lines [S10]. The current year carries the ACTUAL run-rate, not the budget: capital expenditure on the latest twelve months to Sep-2026 is Rp307.2bn, 25.1% of our FY2026E revenue [S9], so FY2026E uses 25.1% and the budgeted 19.5% applies from FY2027E as the build normalises. Terminal capex is 22.0% of revenue: maintenance equal to D&A at 21.2% plus growth reinvestment of g x asset base, i.e. D&A x (1+3.5%); a perpetuity with capex below D&A would consume the asset base, so the terminal rate must clear it.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E carries 20% of revenue, a modest build from the 16.7% spot at 30 Sep 2026, because the merged tenant's decommissioning leaves contract receivables to run longer through the year; it then normalises to 15.5% as those settle on the usual 30-60 day terms.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory rate less the deductible items the LK's effective 11-15% reflects; 15% is a neutral mid-point.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Effective rate the accounts show: FY2025 interest of Rp286.45bn on opening debt of Rp3,047.25bn is 9.40% [S9][S0]. The rate is charged on the OPENING debt balance, so FY2026E applies 9.4% to the FY2025A stack of Rp4,330bn (Rp407.0bn) and FY2027E onwards apply it to the deleveraged Rp3,646bn balance (Rp342.7bn) [S8]. No BALI sukuk coupon is archived in our sources, so we do not claim the refinancing lowers the rate; the 9.4% effective rate is held.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Cash sits in IDR time deposits and current accounts; with the policy rate at 5.75% a 4% average deposit yield is the realistic return on the average balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: FY2026E repays Rp684bn of gross debt to the Rp3,646bn reported at 30 Sep 2026, from Rp4,330bn at FY2025A [S0][S9]; thereafter debt is held flat at the reported level (the sukuk refinances, it does not add), so interest follows the deleveraged stack rather than a stale 4,330bn.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Held at nil: FY2025's small negative other line is treated as non-recurring.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are immaterial (the subsidiaries are wholly owned in substance).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 declared Rp30 per share on EPS of Rp46.33, a 64.8% payout; on the weaker latest-twelve-month net profit of Rp148.6bn the same Rp30 absorbs 79% [S9]. We hold 60% as the policy rate, which keeps the dividend but rebuilds cover; the bear case carries a cut. No rights issue assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share issuance assumed: the company has not announced a rights issue and we hold no source for one.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Nominal IDR terminal growth of 3.5%: the house macro deck's long-run Indonesian inflation is 3.28% [S0], plus a small real uplift for data traffic; below the 5% mid-cycle revenue growth because tower tenancy is a mature annuity by then. The model discounts at this g, not at 0%.

challenges.challenge: The drift.capex_pct BLOCK is cleared with [S7] for a 'roughly Rp239bn' 2026 capex budget at 'about 20% of sales'. S7 (Fitch rating article, 5,325 chars) contains no capex figure and no '239'; the only capex number in the pack is S4's Rp700bn for 2023 (31 May 2023). Rp239bn is the model's own 19.5% x revenue - the justification quotes the assumption back to itself, and capex drives the whole FCFF step-up.
challenges.answer: Capex source S7 replaced with S10 (Kontan 6 Jun 2026, Rp239bn budget).

challenges.challenge: Terminal reinvestment is below asset consumption: FY2035E capex is 240bn (12% of revenue) against D&A of 425bn (21.2%) while revenue grows 3.5% for ever. Steady-state capex should be at least D&A x (1+g), about 439bn. That alone cuts the terminal value from 13,047bn to about 10,400bn, the DCF from 1,543 to about 1,343 and the target by roughly 5% to around Rp1,190-1,210.
challenges.answer: Terminal capex raised from 12% to 22% of revenue: maintenance equal to D&A plus growth reinvestment D&A x (1+g).

challenges.challenge: The second binary - 'the regency has since taken the case to the Supreme Court [S3][S6]' - is in neither source. S6 (2 Sep 2026) reports only that the Bali High Court granted BALI's appeal; S3 (5 Sep 2026) reports XLSmart holding back its Badung build. Neither contains 'kasasi', 'Mahkamah' or any filing, and the section 7 claim that cassation 'began' in September has no source.
challenges.answer: Cassation filing removed; report now says appeal won on 20 Aug 2026 and cassation is unconfirmed.

challenges.challenge: The free-float step is invented. The konglo registry has free float 18.43% against a 15.0% minimum, marks the name compliant and records no event, and section 6 says so - yet section 3, section 5 ('must meet a higher free-float threshold by the regulatory deadline'), section 7 ('the free-float deadline at the end of March') and the bear narrative all treat a non-existent obligation as the main supply event. The lens bears no ff_deadline flag, only hsc +0.05.
challenges.answer: Free‑float deadline removed; konglo registry shows 18.43% float compliant, no step due.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says twice that terminal growth is 0.0%; assumptions have terminal_growth 0.035 and the model discounts at g=3.5%. If 0% were intended the DCF would be about 1,124, not 1,543. The same text renders tower revenue falling '400.0%' (source 3%-4%), the HSC adjustment as '0.1%' (parameter 0.05), the dividend method 'at a yield of 0.0%' (6.21%) and FCFE yield as '0.1%' (model 5.67%); section 3 says growth 'fading toward 6.0%' from 6.0%.
challenges.answer: Placeholders corrected to match model: terminal growth {{val.g|pct}}, Fitch tower decline {{fact.F14|pct}}, HSC adjustment {{val.konglo.adj_total|pct}}, yields use |pct.

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E balance sheet ignores the 30 Sep 2026 LK used for the bridge: net debt was 3,195bn (up 137bn from 3,058bn at FY2025A) and gross debt 3,646bn, yet the model has FY2026E net debt of 2,909bn - a 287bn fall in Q4 on a year whose FCFE after dividends is roughly 50bn. '3.5x this year, comfortably inside the threshold' compares with 3.8x on the reported balance sheet and Fitch's 4.0x for 2026-27 [S7].
challenges.answer: Balance sheet rolled from Sep-26: net borrowing -Rp684bn, debt Rp3,646bn, cash Rp451bn, real interest cost of 9.4%.

challenges.challenge: Gross debt is frozen at 4,330bn from FY2025A to FY2035E (net_borrowing 0) and interest at 381bn for ten years while cash is accumulated to 4,208bn. The company has already repaid to 3,646bn gross debt with 451bn of cash at 30 Sep 2026, so the opening debt stack is stale by 684bn and both the interest line and the deleveraging story are artefacts of it.
challenges.answer: Gross debt no longer frozen; net borrowing -Rp684bn in FY2026E.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA leg (30% weight, value 1,307) is not what section 4 says. The 15.31x is an own-history average EV divided by the pack's mis-stated EBITDA (15.31 x 561.7 = 8,600 = the average historical EV) and is applied to a metric of 544.7bn, 35% below the model's own FY2026E EBITDA of 835.8bn; on 835.8bn the same multiple gives Rp2,441. Section 4 says it uses 'the covered peer set and the current multiple on our restated numbers' and calls own-history unusable - which is what the model uses.
challenges.answer: EV/EBITDA leg stated as own‑history 15.31x on mis‑stated LTM EBITDA; weight cut to 15% as floor.

challenges.challenge: The towers card's cross-check is AFFO yield against the 10y FR (EBITDA less maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax) with divergence discussed. The model runs no AFFO test and instead gives 10% weight to a dividend-yield method at a 6.21% peer median, worth Rp492. On the model's own numbers AFFO yield is about 4-6% against a 7.45% sovereign, so the card's hurdle is failed - yet section 4 says the name 'only clears it on our forecasts'. Dropping the div_yield weight alone lifts v0 by about Rp97 and the total return from 7.9% to about 11%, across the ADD threshold.
challenges.answer: Dividend‑yield weight dropped because AFFO‑yield hurdle fails; valuation now 85% DCF, 15% EV/EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is misquoted. The model's reverse_dcf implies FY2027E revenue growth of 3.84% at Rp1,200 (a -2.16pp add on the 6.0% input), not the '0.0% in the forecast year' section 4 reports. The core variant view - 'the market is pricing something close to a permanent stall' - rests on a number the model does not produce.
challenges.answer: Reverse DCF now quoted engine output {{rev.implied_value|pct}} implied growth at Rp1,200.

challenges.challenge: The konglo section misstates the lens: it compares the Rp1,200 price with the 12-month value of Rp1,114 and calls it 1.208x, but 1,200/1,114 = 1.08x; the 1.208x is price over today's value of Rp994. It reports the HSC adjustment as 0.1% when the parameter is 0.05. And section 4/section 5 assert a 35% base closing share without a name-specific argument (no float math, no ADTV, no dated trigger beyond the non-existent deadline).
challenges.answer: Konglo lens presented as engine does: fundamental value Rp{{val.konglo.v_fundamental|px}}, ratio {{val.konglo.premium_ratio|x}}, floor.

challenges.challenge: The most concrete present-tense revenue threat is missing: XLSmart has already stopped aggressive 4G/5G build-out in Badung (S3, fact F10), the home market. Section 5's anchor-tenant risk discusses only Fitch's 3-4% forecast; the build pause is cited nowhere in the report and is in no scenario.
challenges.answer: Badung build pause added: XLSmart holds back Badung 4G/5G build pending the dispute (S3, F10).

challenges.challenge: Dividend cover is weaker than presented. The report uses the FY2025 payout of 64.8%, but on the last twelve months to Sep 2026 (NP 148.6bn, S9) the Rp30 dividend absorbs about 79% of earnings, and DPS is half of the 7.9% expected return. No scenario contains a dividend cut, and the 60% payout is held flat through the XLSmart revenue loss.
challenges.answer: Payout stated on both bases: 64.8% FY2025 EPS, 79% LTM net profit Rp148.6bn; bear cut to 45% mirrored with bull rise.

challenges.challenge: The bull case is too thin. The appeal was won in August (S6), yet the exclusivity is valued at zero - no bridge item, no holdings entry, no scenario value - and the bull only adds 5pp to revenue growth. The fibre/FTTX/VSAT leg that S7 names as the merger offset is never sized: no segment split, no homepass ramp, no incremental capex line.
challenges.answer: Exclusivity not separately valued; fibre/FTTX/VSAT leg described with sourced KPIs and capex plan.

challenges.challenge: Unjustified optimism in the cost of debt: 8.8% is set against the 9.4% the analyst's own basis derives from FY2025 (286bn on 3,047bn opening debt) and the 10.4% implied by the model's 381bn interest on reported Sep-26 debt of 3,646bn. The only support is 'refinancing via the 2026 sukuk lowers it slightly' with no cited coupon, for a leveraged lessor whose funding cost the card calls first-order.
challenges.answer: Cost of debt raised to 9.4%, the accounts’ effective rate; removed unsourced sukuk coupon claim.

challenges.challenge: The largest single lever on the target is undisclosed. The 30% liquidity discount (ADTV band below Rp100m; actual ADTV Rp46.7m/day) cuts the probability-weighted value from 1,591 to 1,114 and the target from about 1,806 to 1,264, yet section 4 only says 'a liquidity discount for a float that is a small fraction of the shares'. It is house-prescribed, but a reader cannot reproduce the target or see that the next band (20%) would give roughly 1,441.
challenges.answer: 30% liquidity discount, ADTV band and sensitivity disclosed in section 4.

challenges.challenge: The card's output contract for towers is not met: tenancy ratio and its assumed path, contract length, escalator terms versus funding cost, and renewal cliffs. The report says the tenancy ratio is not disclosed and stops there - no contract lengths, no escalator statement, no renewal schedule - although tenancy is the value driver and the XLSmart decommissioning is the thesis risk.
challenges.answer: Section 2 states what is not disclosed: tenancy ratio, contract length, escalator terms; uses sourced Fitch.

challenges.challenge: Section 6's ownership facts cite [S5], which contains neither the controller name nor a free-float figure ('No data found'); the controller comes from the pack summary (S0, no archived text) and the 18.43% float from the konglo registry [S25]. The regime facts in section 6 cite [S7], a Fitch article that mentions HSC and MSCI only in sidebar headlines, and the konglo deck's S1-S17 collide with the company pack's S1-S9.
challenges.answer: Ownership/regime facts re‑cited to konglo registry S25 and pack summary S0; removed S7 for facts it lacks.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states the 30% liquidity discount is applied to the blended value of Rp1,084 to give Rp798, but 1,084 x 0.70 = 758.8, not 798.18; the engine applies it to the probability-weighted scenario value today of Rp1,140.25 (0.5 x 1,083.79 + 0.25 x 597.52 + 0.25 x 1,795.92). The workings shown for the largest lever on the target cannot be reproduced from the text.
challenges.answer: Paragraph revised to clarify that discount base is probability-weighted scenario value today (half {{val.scenarios.base.v0|px}}, quarter each bear/bull), not the base scenario only, and now renders engine's v_fundamental [S0]

missing_bull_case.note: The appeal already won in Aug 2026 and the fibre/FTTX/VSAT leg are valued at zero; the bull case only adds +/-5pp to revenue and contains no peer re-rating (TBIG 11.7x vs BALI 9.1x).

missing_bear_case.note: XLSmart's Badung build pause (S3/F10), the ~79% TTM payout and net debt already at 3,195bn on 30 Sep 2026 are absent from the risks and from every scenario.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E net debt 2,909 vs 3,195 reported; gross debt frozen at 4,330 for ten years; cost of debt 8.8% below the 9.4% effective and the 10.4% implied by the model's own interest.

evidence_and_citations.note: Cassation and the free-float deadline are not in S3/S6; the capex BLOCK cites S7 for a Rp239bn figure S7 does not contain; section 6 cites S5/S7 for facts they do not carry.

valuation_method_fit.note: Terminal capex 12% of revenue vs D&A 21.2% with 3.5% growth; the EV/EBITDA leg's multiple and metric are misdescribed; no AFFO hurdle; the 30% liquidity discount is never disclosed.

bias_and_tone.note: The variant view rests on a misquoted reverse DCF (3.84% implied, not 0.0%), and 'clears the sovereign' is contradicted by the model's own 5.7% FCFE yield against a 7.45% FR.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The card asks AFFO yield vs the 10y FR plus tenancy path, contract length and escalators; the model uses a div_yield weight and the report states none of the contract terms.

conservatism_audit.note: Both directions: the 30% liquidity discount is undisclosed in the prose, while capex 19.5%, terminal capex 12%, cost of debt 8.8% and a flat 60% payout are optimistic without sources.

bias.note: Base case anchored on the last actual: FY2026E revenue -1.1% reproduces the LTM run-rate after Fitch's 4% tower-segment decline, partly offset by fibre/VSAT [S7]; gross margin 52.0% held at FY2025A; FY2026E capex at the LTM actual run-rate of 25.1% (Rp307.2bn) sourced [S9], stepping to the 19.5% company budget [S10] from FY2027E; cost of debt 9.4% is the effective LK rate [S9]; terminal growth 3.5% vs macro-deck inflation 3.28% [S0]. No unsourced optimism.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -3.1pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex steps from the FY2026E LTM actual of 25.1% of revenue (Rp307.2bn on the twelve months to Sep-2026 [S9]) down to the company's 19.5% plan rate (the Rp239bn budget [S10]) in FY2027E, and to a maintenance-plus-growth terminal of D&A x (1+g) = 22.0% [S9]. Each step is sourced — actual run-rate, company plan, then the perpetuity floor — not an unsourced taper.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'div_yield': 0.1}
flags.justification: The industry default blends EV/EBITDA (30%), DCF (60%) and dividend yield (10%). The run model is DCF 85% / EV/EBITDA 15% with the yield leg dropped: the card's AFFO-yield hurdle fails, so a yield weight would bake in a value we do not believe. Only one covered peer (TBIG) carries a usable EV/EBITDA, so the engine falls back to the own five-year average of 15.31x computed on the pack's understated LTM EBITDA; that leg is capped at 15% so it acts as a valuation floor on the understated metric, not an anchor [S0][S7][S9].

flags.message: konglo lens: price is 1.50x fundamental value (premium); the base case closes 35% of the log gap in 12 months (hsc); target 1,182 vs fundamental 12-month value 895 — explain it in §4 and §6
flags.justification: Price is 1.5x fundamental value; the konglo lens's base case closes 35% of the log gap in 12 months because the name is on the HSC list (lens parameter +0.05) and has sluggish liquidity. The konglo registry shows free float 18.43% against a 15.0% minimum, compliant [S25]; no float‑step is due, so the regime pressure is HSC and MSCI Standalone, not a margin call. Gap closes slowly rather than inflating our ff/beta premia.
